strengths: The paper proposes a useful combination of density-ratio Bayesian optimization with label propagation and label spreading. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools gives the approach practical scope, particularly when candidate features are available before expensive evaluations.

The empirical study includes BORE and LFBO with four classifier families, GP-EI/UCB, and several benchmark families. Twenty repetitions with standard-error bands strengthen the evidence. Figures 2–3 show substantial improvements on several synthetic tasks, and Figure 6 demonstrates faster convergence on NATS-Bench.

The appendices investigate bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled sample counts, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios. Including a no-transduction control and acknowledging both computational limitations and the inapplicability of existing i.i.d. theory are valuable aspects of the analysis.
weaknesses: The central benefit attributed to unlabeled-data propagation is insufficiently isolated. In Figure 12, the no-transduction control is competitive or better in several cases, notably Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. These experiments fix beta=0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta each iteration. Consequently, the results do not establish how much improvement comes from propagation versus the kernel surrogate, bandwidth selection, or random tie-breaking. A comparably tuned supervised kernel classifier and ablations separating these components are important for substantiating the contribution.

The explanation for improved exploration remains largely conjectural. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed inputs does not establish the cluster assumption: high-density connections can cross the objective's changing good/bad threshold. Appendix D asserts that propagation can expand the favorable decision region by reducing a margin, but does not establish this behavior or connect it to better optimization. Its cited guarantees are explicitly inapplicable to adaptive sampling. The proposed mechanism needs stronger objective-related assumptions or direct measurements of exploration and escape from local optima.

Acquisition optimization is insufficiently specified to assess comparison fairness. Section 5 describes L-BFGS-B with 1,000 initializations, but does not adequately explain selection from arbitrary finite pools, corresponding optimization procedures for tree acquisitions, or whether candidate restrictions and plateau tie-breaking are consistent across methods. These choices can materially affect the reported performance. A random-search baseline is also missing, particularly relevant for the newly introduced pool-search task.

The MNIST experiment provides limited evidence for general high-dimensional black-box optimization. Appendix E.4 trains the embedding network on 440,000 images labeled with the same three-digit quantity subsequently optimized. This supplies substantial supervised information about the objective, even with the documented separate test split. Comparing against direct ranking using the pretrained classifier would clarify the value added by optimization. The continuous sampling experiments otherwise cover only four two-dimensional functions.

Important reproduction details remain missing, including feature scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, bandwidth initialization and bounds, and several baseline training settings. Feature scaling is particularly consequential for the isotropic RBF kernel and identity-covariance sampling. Figure 14 studies runtime versus subset size, but does not establish comparative end-to-end costs for the main configuration with learned bandwidth.

A minor mathematical inconsistency should be corrected: the stated column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P=WD^{-1}, whereas Section 4.1 states P=D^{-1}W and subsequently propagates using P transpose. Clarifying the intended normalization would make the implemented algorithm unambiguous.
